name: Hosted Reading Sync (KOReader-compatible)
idea: A free hosted progress-sync endpoint for KOReader e-reader users plus a browser dashboard of reading stats, so nobody has to self-host a sync server.
description: Gives each reader a personal sync account whose address they paste into KOReader; progress per book is stored as tiny rows and shown on a web dashboard. Users can also drop their KOReader statistics file into the page and get charts computed entirely in the browser. Aimed at e-ink readers who want position sync across devices without Docker. Hard to copy because the sync protocol has device/document-hash quirks and the stats file is an obscure SQLite schema.
web_delivery: Vercel serverless routes implement the sync HTTP API against Supabase Postgres (one small row per user+book); dashboard is a normal web app; statistics.sqlite is parsed client-side with sql.js (WASM). No file storage needed.
why_hard_to_copy: Needs wire-compatibility with an existing device-side protocol (document hashing, never-sync-backwards rules) and parsing of KOReader's statistics database client-side; niche e-reader knowledge most vibe coders lack.

signals.summary: Users reported that KOReader's progress sync server could not be pushed to or pulled from on Pocketbook and Android; the long thread later turned into an OTA-server outage discussion, showing how fragile the single default sync server is.
Request to improve the automatic progress-sync experience, which is cumbersome especially when there is no WiFi connection.

Asks the Calibre-Web-Automated library server to sync reading progress with KOReader devices; a second thread (issue 461, 2025-08-02) asks the same for its web reader. Both still active in 2026 (last updated 2026-01-29 and 2026-05-10).
Long-running request to sync reading position between devices logged into the same account; still being updated in 2026 (last update 2026-08-03).
Top request on Audiobookshelf to sync ebooks to Kobo e-readers; still receiving comments in Sept 2026, including a community member who built a small bridge because the feature does not exist.

name: MediaMover
idea: A browser tool that imports exports from Trakt, Letterboxd, TV Time, StoryGraph, Goodreads and others into one clean library and exports back out to any of them.
description: Users drop their export files into the page; parsers normalise titles, dates, ratings and rewatch counts, match them against open metadata, and let the user review low-confidence matches. The result is a shareable read-only library page plus export files in the format of any target service. Aimed at people leaving or hedging against a tracker that changes pricing or shuts down. The moat is the pile of obscure export formats and matching edge cases.
web_delivery: Static web app with all parsing and matching UI in the browser; Supabase stores only the user's optional shareable library JSON; Vercel serves the pages and a small metadata proxy route.
why_hard_to_copy: Many undocumented export formats, season/episode and edition mapping edge cases, and fuzzy matching with a review step; accumulating tested parsers takes real time.

name: Upkeep Planner
idea: A home maintenance planner where recurring chores are generated per appliance and per season, and the next due date counts from when you actually did it.
description: Add the appliances and parts of your home, pick from a hand-curated library of maintenance tasks with sensible intervals, and get a calendar with reminders that reschedule from completion. Also tracks lent-out items with return reminders. For homeowners and renters who find general to-do apps too dumb for recurring care. The curated task library and correct recurrence rules are the moat.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel with Supabase auth and Postgres; reminders via email using Supabase scheduled functions or push for installed PWAs; task library shipped as JSON seeds.
why_hard_to_copy: A hand-curated, region- and climate-aware task and interval library plus a recurrence engine that handles 'after completion', seasonal windows and skipped cycles.

name: Kinship Explorer
idea: Upload a GEDCOM file and see exactly how any two people in the tree are related, including in-laws and step relatives, with culture-aware names and kinship terms.
description: Everything runs in the browser: parse the family tree file, pick two people, and get the path, the relationship name in the user's language, and a diagram. Name display can follow local conventions such as patronymics or surname-first order. Anniversary and birthday lists can be exported as a calendar file. Hard to copy because kinship terms and name conventions differ by culture and in-law logic is fiddly.
web_delivery: Static web app on Vercel; GEDCOM parsed and queried entirely in the browser (no upload, no storage); Supabase only for optional saved views and share links.
why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical kinship logic (half, step, in-law, multiple spouses) plus per-language relationship terms and name-order formats; client-side parsing of messy GEDCOM variants.

signals.summary: Wants a diagram showing how two specific people are related. Comments on 2026-10-15 show the maintainer undecided on the UI and the requester insisting it must work for any two people, not only the home person.

name: Open Language Reader
idea: A browser reader where you import a text, click any word for a definition, track known words, and get proper word splitting for languages like Korean, Japanese and Thai.
description: Paste text, upload an EPUB, or load subtitles; words are segmented using the browser's built-in segmenter, looked up in downloadable dictionary packs that work offline, and graded known/learning/unknown. Study progress and streaks are kept per language. Aimed at self-directed language learners who outgrew flashcards. The per-language segmentation and offline dictionary packs are the moat.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel; text and vocabulary in IndexedDB with optional Supabase sync; dictionary packs fetched once from static hosting and cached; segmentation uses the browser's Intl.Segmenter plus small bundled tokenizers.
why_hard_to_copy: Per-language tokenization edge cases, curated offline dictionary packs, and EPUB/subtitle parsing, all client-side.

name: FreeBusy Hub
idea: Combine all your calendars into one subscribable feed that shows only busy blocks, with a per-calendar choice of what details to reveal.
description: Paste the private ICS links of your work, personal and family calendars; the service expands recurring events correctly and publishes a single secret feed URL (and a small availability page) that shows 'busy' or selected details only. Aimed at people who juggle work and private calendars, freelancers, and families that share one availability view. The moat is correct recurrence and timezone handling across messy real-world feeds.

why_hard_to_copy: Correctness-critical iCalendar handling: recurrence expansion, timezone definitions, all-day and multi-day edge cases, and CLASS/transparency fields that vary between providers.

name: MealMerge
idea: A meal planner whose shopping list correctly adds up the same ingredient across recipes, converts units, and optionally subtracts what is in your pantry.
description: Plan the week from your saved recipes and get one shopping list where 2 eggs plus 3 eggs becomes 5, grams and cups are reconciled by ingredient, and pantry items can be taken off. why_hard_to_copy: Accurate ingredient parsing and unit/density conversion across metric and imperial with fuzzy ingredient matching; a hand-built conversion table is slow to get right.

name: Night Shift Baby Log
idea: A shared baby tracker PWA that works offline at 3am, handles daylight-saving time properly, plots WHO growth percentiles, and lets parents add their own event types.
description: Two or more caregivers log feeds (including which breast was last), sleep, diapers, medication doses and custom events such as reflux or bath, all synced in real time and usable offline. Shows wake windows, growth percentile charts and a one-page summary for the paediatrician. Aimed at new parents who do not want ads or a paid sharing tier. The moat is correct time handling plus real-time offline sync and growth-chart data.
web_delivery: Offline-first PWA on Vercel; Supabase Realtime and Postgres for multi-caregiver sync; local queue in IndexedDB for offline logging; growth percentile tables bundled as static data.
why_hard_to_copy: Offline-first sync with conflict handling for running timers, DST/timezone-correct durations, and percentile (growth chart) data and calculations.

name: Plant Care Library
idea: A free plant care library with watering, light and soil guidance per species, plus reminders that adapt to your room and season, usable as a plain web app.
description: Search a species (or pick from a curated starter list), add the plant to a room, and get care reminders with intervals based on light, pot size and season rather than a flat every-7-days. Includes pet-toxicity flags and a 'what went wrong' checker for yellow or drooping leaves. Aimed at houseplant owners who find paid apps pushy. The moat is the curated species care dataset, not the app shell.
web_delivery: PWA on Vercel; species dataset as static JSON built from open data (e.g. open plant databases) and hand-checked; Supabase for user plants and reminders; email or web-push reminders.
why_hard_to_copy: Hand-curated and verified care dataset with adaptive interval rules; external plant APIs used by self-hosted apps have proved unreliable or paid.

name: Shared Private Journal
idea: A shared journal for couples, families or travel groups where entries are encrypted in the browser so even the host cannot read them.
description: Create a journal, invite a partner or family, and write entries that are encrypted with a key shared only among members, with a recovery option. Entries can carry a place so a map view shows where memories happened. Aimed at people who want a private shared diary without paying for Day One's premium. The moat is trustworthy multi-member end-to-end encryption and key recovery done right in the browser.
web_delivery: Web app/PWA on Vercel; WebCrypto for client-side encryption with per-journal keys wrapped per member; Supabase stores only ciphertext; photos kept small and limited to stay in free storage.
why_hard_to_copy: Multi-user key management, invitations, rotation and recovery are security-critical and easy to get wrong; most vibe-coded clones skip real encryption.

signals.summary: Asks to share a journal with other users for collaborative journals such as family or travel journals; updated 2026-04-07.
Points out entries are stored in plain text in the database and asks for encryption, which matters if hosting for other people.
Asks to encrypt everything with a password; updated 2026-08-18.
Wants location data shown in entries and a map view of journal entries; updated 2026-07-15.

name: Volunteer Rota
idea: A volunteer and club rota builder that fills shifts automatically from people's availability and handles swaps and find-a-sub requests.
description: Organisers list roles and dates, volunteers mark when they cannot serve, and the tool proposes a fair rota; volunteers accept, decline or ask for a substitute from a simple link, no app install. Aimed at small churches, clubs, food banks and school groups that outgrew spreadsheets. The moat is the fairness-aware auto-fill logic with constraints, which is real scheduling logic rather than CRUD.
web_delivery: Web app on Vercel with Supabase; constraint-based auto-fill runs in the browser or a serverless function; magic-link responses and calendar feed per volunteer.
why_hard_to_copy: Constraint scheduling (availability, blackout dates, fairness, team balance) and swap workflows are correctness-critical, unlike a simple signup sheet.

signals.summary: The ChurchCRM maintainers opened an epic to redesign volunteer management around self-service scheduling, showing the existing volunteer tools were not enough.
Planning documentation of the workflow where a volunteer accepts, declines or finds a substitute from a member portal.
Asks for a ready-to-run Docker image to help testers and less-technical installer teams, signalling that small churches struggle to self-host.

name: Trip Log
idea: A travel log that imports saved places from Google Maps exports and GPX files, with per-visit notes, time-zone-correct itineraries and a calendar feed.
description: Drop a Google Takeout saved-places file or GPX tracks and see them as visits on a map, attach notes to each visit rather than the place, and build multi-day itineraries where every leg shows the correct local time. Export the plan as a calendar file. Aimed at travellers who keep lists in Google Maps and want a structured record. The moat is the import parsers and time-zone-correct itinerary logic.
web_delivery: Web app on Vercel; Takeout and GPX parsed client-side; maps via free open tile sources; Supabase stores trips as text/JSON with no heavy media hosting.
why_hard_to_copy: Obscure export format parsing done entirely in the browser plus timezone-aware multi-leg itinerary logic.

signals.summary: Wants automatic import of saved-place collections from Google Maps because hundreds of saved places are part of the travel workflow.
